questions.question: Describe the sequence by which a thermal power station produces electricity, trace the energy conversions and the main loss, and explain why such stations suit base load.
questions.expected_answer: Heat from the fuel boils water in a boiler into high-pressure steam; the steam rushes through a turbine, a shaft of blade rows, spinning it at three thousand revolutions a minute; the turbine turns a generator in which a rotating magnet inside coils drives alternating current; transformers raise the voltage to hundreds of thousands of volts for the grid; and the used steam is condensed back to water, in South Africa mostly by air in concrete cooling towers whose white plumes are water vapour, while smoke leaves through tall stacks. Chemical, nuclear or radiant energy becomes heat, heat becomes the kinetic energy of steam, steam energy becomes rotational energy of the turbine, and rotation becomes electrical energy in the generator, with losses at each step and the largest in the condenser where remaining heat is discarded, so a good coal station converts thirty-five to forty percent of fuel energy to electricity, a limit set by heat-engine physics. Because boilers take hours to heat and turbines must be brought up carefully, thermal stations run continuously and adjust slowly, suiting the steady base load; a large unit gives 600 to 800 megawatts and Medupi or Kusile with six units gives about 4800 megawatts, burning a trainload of coal every hour or two.

questions.question: Explain how coal, gas and nuclear stations produce their heat and set out the advantages and disadvantages of each in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Coal is crushed to powder and burned in the boiler, supplying about eighty percent of South Africa's electricity from large Mpumalanga and Limpopo stations; its advantages are abundant cheap local fuel with no imports, existing stations and skills, reliable base load and tens of thousands of jobs, while its disadvantages are the highest carbon dioxide, sulphur and nitrogen oxides, particulates, mercury and ash, among the world's worst air quality on the Highveld, heavy water use, mining scars and acid drainage, an ageing unreliable fleet behind load shedding, and a cost now above new wind and solar. Gas, mostly methane, is burned in gas turbines like jet engines driving generators, with exhaust heat boiling water for a second turbine in combined cycle; advantages are about half coal's carbon dioxide, little sulphur or ash, start-up in minutes to follow demand and back up renewables, and fast construction, while disadvantages are scarce domestic gas requiring dollar-priced imports by pipeline or ship, methane leakage as a potent greenhouse gas, and remaining a fossil fuel; South Africa's Ankerlig and Gourikwa turbines burn costly diesel only at peaks. Nuclear at Koeberg splits uranium in a reactor heating pressurised water that heats a separate steam loop; advantages are no carbon dioxide or smoke in operation, tiny fuel quantities for 1800 megawatts, high reliability and long life, while disadvantages are very high construction cost and time, radioactive waste requiring storage for millennia, a small risk of catastrophic accident demanding strict regulation, large cooling water needs met by the sea, and public distrust.

questions.question: Describe concentrating solar thermal power with its advantages and disadvantages, compare the four heat sources on common criteria, and state a balanced judgement.
questions.expected_answer: Concentrating solar thermal stations use parabolic troughs to focus sunlight onto oil-filled pipes or thousands of tracking heliostats to focus it onto a tower receiver heating molten salt to several hundred degrees, which boils water for an ordinary steam cycle; South Africa has tower plants near Upington and trough plants near Pofadder. Advantages are free clean fuel in one of the sunniest regions on earth and molten salt storage that allows generation for hours after sunset into the evening peak; disadvantages are higher cost per unit than photovoltaics, no output in prolonged cloud, large land and some water use, and an immature technology with teething troubles. On common criteria, coal has cheap local fuel, gas imported fuel, uranium small partly imported quantities and sun free fuel; coal and nuclear give steady but slow base load, gas is fast and flexible, solar thermal gives daytime plus stored hours; coal is worst for air pollution and carbon, gas about half, nuclear and solar thermal near zero in operation; coal, nuclear and solar thermal need cooling water; coal leaves ash mountains, nuclear small but millennia-dangerous waste, solar little; coal kills steadily through pollution and mining while nuclear rarely but catastrophically; building cost is moderate for coal and gas, very high for nuclear, high but falling for solar thermal; coal employs most today. The balanced judgement is that South Africa depends on coal and cannot switch it off overnight, but ageing, polluting, costly coal should be replaced over time by cheap solar and wind, storage, flexible gas, possibly extended nuclear and solar thermal for evenings, while supporting coal communities in a just transition.
